newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan bearish with Dow at 6,000; bullish at 8,000.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan bearish with Dow at 6,000; bullish at 8,000.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, the Emperor of interest rates, resurfaced, but this time he used a different E word, sidestepping the "exuberance" of the stock market and proclaiming that "exceptional" things are happening to the economy.
But Wall Streeters are nervous and some wonder if it's a good or bad omen for stocks now that Greenspan, who was bearish on a 6,000-point Dow, has turned bullish at 8,000.
Greenspan's uncharacteristically upbeat comments about the economy shocked the stock market and sent the Dow Jones industrial average whirling to three straight days of record highs this past week.

In late afternoon trading Friday, the world's most closely watched gauge of 30 blue-chip stocks was unchanged at 8,116.93, holding at the previous day's record close. For the week, it was up a solid 226.47 points.

Investors were on the edge of their seats, expecting the Fed chief to drop another bombshell that would rock financial markets in Congressional testimony during his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins report on the economy.
In the past, Greenspan has had problems explaining why the economy has been growing strongly without a hint of inflation for six years, which has sent stocks gushing higher.

The market is sensitive to hints of rising interest rates. In March, the Fed upped interest rates as a pre-emptive move to head off what it perceived as inflation pressures, triggering a 700-point plunge in the Dow index.

The Fed has cooled its heels since, but analysts were betting last week that Greenspan might cause another stock setback, as he did in December with his remark in a speech about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
But this time, he suggested the economy might be undergoing some "basic improvements" thanks to technological advances that were boosting worker productivity and corporate profits.
"The recent performance of the economy, characterised by strong growth and low inflation, has been exceptional -- and better than most anticipated," Greenspan said.
The head of the central bank told the market what it wanted to hear, raising expectations that stocks could go higher.
Greenspan seemed to recognise that the market and economic fundamentals have changed and the technology revolution may be providing economic bonuses.
But there was also a view that the Fed chief has had to concede that noone is bigger than the stock market.

Despite his past pronouncements, which were aimed at "talking" the market down by getting investors to wonder whether high stock valuations were over-shooting corporate profits, Greenspan still could not mess with market forces.
The legion of investors soon answered Greenspan's famous comments about exuberant markets by giddily boosting the Dow index 1,700 points higher than in December.
This week, Greenspan chose the strategic move of "going" with the durable stock market, preferring to endorse rather than to fight one of the biggest bull market in history.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany Corp. said Greenspan has now acknowledged that he was wrong when he talked about the market's irrational exuberance.

"He tip-toed his way through it, and his statement seemed to have that 'New Economy' lean to it ... and the lower deficits, more investments in technology and productivity and globalization could go for some time."

Billions of dollars have been pouring into stocks over the past two years and investors' sentiment is still positive as corporate earnings continue to meet or exceed expectations. Prior to the start of the market's runup in 1990, earnings tended to miss their goals.
Investors have pumped, on average, $4 billion weekly into stock mutual funds vs. just $1 billion before the market started roaring up 6-1/2 years ago.
But some analysts are worried that the capitulation of a major diehard market bear might be a sign that the bull market may be getting its last gasp.
Now, the concern is that Greenspan's words may unleash a flood of buying by small speculators, who traditionally are the last group to participate in a major market move.
Analysts are watching for any warning signs that a major correction may be waiting in the wings.

A classic contrarian rule says that if 90 percent of the people are going in one direction, then the market is primed for a big move in the other direction. If the whole world is buying, the only decision they can make is to sell.

"When optimism becomes too widespread, yes, it's always a very bad sign," said Johnson. "Right now, I would not say that optimism is one-sided but it's certainly rising and it is bordering on euphoria."
He said that for the last two years, the market has been a money-making machine.

"It's been a wonderful virtuous circle with individuals buying mutual funds and funds buying stocks and as the market is driven higher, it has encouraged people to buy even more funds," he said. "It's been breathtaking and it seems endless."
Talk about exuberance!
